### Justification for choice of study

I choose a recent paper from my advisor. I will try to replicate experiment in the figure 6 (especially the figure 6C). Figure 6C is part of a study analyzing gaze behavior in freely moving marmosets wearing the CEREBRO head-mounted eye-tracking system. The experiment involves recording marmosets as they freely explore a large open arena (200 cm × 100 cm × 240 cm). The goal of the experiment is to test the relations of eye movement and head movement. During this exploration, the system simultaneously records. CERBRO in this paper is an effective device that can collect eye-tracking data in free-moving marmoset. In my project, I will also use CERBRO and record the data from free-moving systems and research questions of specific tasks (e.g. social interactions).My research interest stands on natural visual behavior of the marmoset, so get to familiar with the eye-tracking data collected by this device is helpful for me to do research. 

### Anticipated challenges

Firstly is to extract eye-tracking data, and detect eye behaviors,  use a gaze velocity threshold (e.g., ±200°/s) to classify epochs into Gaze shifts(when gaze velocity exceeds the threshold) and Gaze fixations (when gaze velocity is below the threshold). For each time point during the recorded session. Secondly, plot horizontal eye velocity (or position change) on the y-axis and head yaw velocity (or position change) on the x-axis, use a scatter plot to visualize the relationship, with distinct colors for each epoch.. Then, compute the correlation coefficient between eye and head movements separately for fixation and shift epochs.
Challenge: I think the data may be raw data, so it is difficult to Organize and clean the data. And simulate the data also a challenge because the data is complex. The correct visualization of gaze trajectory is also a challenge.

each time points about 0.02s, I will simulate aproximately 10s in each condition.

b2. The parameter values (means, SDs, correlations)

We can't simulate eye-tracking data using normal distribution casue they are time-series data. There are two relations in the two conditions, so we should simulate separately.

In fixation:

Althouth in fixation, the head and eye still move slowly.

Vhead(t) = A Sin(2pi * ft) + nosie
Veye(t) = -r * Vhead(t) + nosie 

each eye or head movement (a saccade or head turn) is represented as a half-sine velocity pulse because sin function is suitble for time series data, A sine wave starts and ends at zero velocity, peaking smoothly in the middle. This pattern likes real-world velocity. Using r to show negative correlation of Veye. Use noise, which is for simulate real world data. The nosie's distribution is N(0, std)

Parameters: A: a reasonable number for fixation head peak velocity, values can caculated by the real data

f: Frequency

-r: correlation r

noise: can estimate by the varience of data


In gaze shift:

in this condition, when the marmosets gaze shifts, it is obviously increase	the value of both velocities, so I give them a pulse, wich represnts the gaze shift.

Vevent_head(t) = Apeak_head Sin(pi * (t-t0/Dhead)) (when the event happens, time:t0, t is only avalible from t0 to t0+ Dhead)

Vevent_eye(t) = Apeak_eye Sin(pi * (t-t0/Deye)) (When the event happens , time:t0, t is only avalible from t0 to t0+ Deye)

So the t is the real time, and when t goes t+D, the event finish. D is the duration of shift.

So the real velcoty is 

Vhead_real(t) = Vhead(t) + Vhead_event(t)
Veye_real(t) = Veye(t) + Veye_event(t)
